newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: FEATURE - Malaysian children compete for stardom.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Malaysian children compete for stardom.

text.p: In a country where skyscrapers boast world titles, some of Malaysia's youngest citizens -- backed by their eager parents -- are reaching for the stars in a bid for their own fame and fortune.
Astronomy? Hardly.
The only stars some Malaysians are keen to uncover are their own offspring, by way of increasingly popular talent contests.
And success, for many, appears to be just one modelling, singing or dancing class away.
"Sometimes when they face the camera, they don't know how to pose, it's not natural, so we will teach them," said Tina Loo, who charges $240 for a series of 12 child model classes.
For that sum, Loo said she teaches her young charges the "basics of modelling", like catwalk work, posing and the art of make-up.
Her trainees start young. One student, Ngeow Sin Kuan, is just three-and-a-half years old. Her mother said she hopes the classes will help her daughter overcome her shyness.
Singing teacher Chong Yoke Mei said children now form the bulk of his students. "I think the reason is because, maybe, the parents like their children to go for public appearances," he said.
SHOPPING CENTRE STAGES
These appearances are usually held at shopping centres, which stage various children's talent shows as a cheap and easy way to draw patrons.

American-style malls have proliferated in Malaysia along with skyscrapers like the 452-metre (1,483 foot) Petronas Twin Towers in the capital Kuala Lumpur -- the world's tallest buildings -- emblematic of the country's thrusting growth.
Six-year-old Julian Toh is a veteran of pageants, having competed for three years. The young beauty queen has won scores of trophies.

Her quest began after her mother noticed her imitating fashion models. "Since she seemed so interested, we decided to register her with a casting agency...and that's how it started," her mother Doreen said.
CONTESTS NEWLY POPULAR

The killing of child beauty pageant contestant Jonbenet Ramsey in the United States recenty has focused global attention on the little-known world of children's beauty contests. Jonbenet was found strangled in the basement of her family's home in Colorado after a kidnapping note was found in the house.
In Malaysia, such competitions are still in their infancy, having captured popular imagination only in the last few years.
Growing affluence and an expanding middle class spurred by nearly a decade of over eight percent growth is making it possible for parents to devote more resources to their children.
SOME SEE NEGATIVE EFFECTS
But some observers believe the focus on such grooming for the sake of competition may have negative effects on the children.

"The satisfaction is more for the parents rather than for the children," said child psychologist Chiam Heng Keng. "I think many of the children do not know what they're doing and they're really being pushed into it."
A FEW ACHIEVE STARDOM
Six-year-old Jasmine Koo has risen from competing in shopping mall pageants to acting in a local television series where she plays the part of the granddaughter of a tycoon.
"Both my husband and I are really happy," gushed her mother. "Jasmine has done the family proud. No one in our family has achieved anything like this, and at such a young age too."
Julian, the pageant champion, may also be tasting stardom. She has been picked by a recording company to be one of the members of a quartet known as "The 4 Princesses".
Whether or not she makes it to that golden pantheon will depend on the sales of the cassette of Chinese children's songs, due to be released soon.
Meanwhile, Julian seems blase about the attention. "I want to become a teacher," she says, when asked about her grown-up ambitions.
Interjected her father: "If she can't become a star, I don't mind if she becomes a teacher."
